title: Unit Count Thresholds: Where Residential Ends and Commercial Begins
summary: Every property gets sorted into one of two worlds the moment you count its units: 1-4, or 5+. That number decides your lender, your valuation method, and your loan type.
body: In real estate, 'residential' and 'commercial' describe two separate financing and valuation systems. The dividing line is unit count: 1 to 4 units is residential (single-family, duplex, triplex, fourplex); 5 or more units is commercial. This is the standard used by Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and FHA in the U.S. Residential properties (1-4 units) are valued using comps -- recent sales of similar nearby properties. Commercial properties (5+ units) are valued using Net Operating Income (NOI) divided by the market cap rate: Value is approximately NOI divided by Cap Rate. Financing also changes: 1-4 units can use conventional, FHA, or VA loans, underwritten mainly on your personal income and credit. 5+ units require commercial financing, underwritten mainly on the property's own income and its Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR), often with higher down payments and shorter loan terms with a balloon payment. The threshold exists because a 1-4 unit property behaves like a home an individual might live in, while a 5+ unit property behaves like a small income-producing business. Key takeaway: know which side of the line a property sits on before you evaluate it -- it determines your entire approach to financing and valuation.

title: VA Loans and Creative Financing: Options at the Residential Threshold
summary: Beyond the conventional mortgage, two other paths open up for residential property: VA loans for eligible veterans, and creative financing that doesn't route through a bank at all.
body: A VA loan is a mortgage backed by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs for eligible veterans, service members, and some surviving spouses, financing 1-4 unit residential properties. It is guaranteed by the VA but originated by a private lender. Key advantages: often no down payment required, no private mortgage insurance (PMI), and competitive rates. This is U.S.-specific and tied to military service. Creative financing is any purchase method that does not rely solely on a bank mortgage, including seller financing (the seller acts as lender), Owner Will Carry (seller carries part or all of the price as a loan), and buyback/leaseback arrangements. In seller financing, buyer and seller negotiate price, down payment, interest rate, and schedule directly; the buyer signs a promissory note and typically a mortgage or deed of trust. Sellers may agree to this for steady income, tax advantages, or a higher effective price; buyers may use it when they don't yet qualify for conventional or VA financing, or want more flexible terms. Creative financing is most useful for specific situations, not a universal first choice -- when a buyer easily qualifies for a low-rate conventional or VA loan, bank financing is usually cheaper and more standardized. Always document creative financing deals with proper legal instruments; informal agreements create real risk for both sides.
